I just finished this game and for a 3-5 hour game, it is full of story in general. Once you get past the "oh it's fake hacking, it's illegal and doesn't serve any meaning," you can truly get a feel for the story. What a great game. I acquired this in a Humble Bundle recently with a few other titles. Without looking, I assumed it was just a game that was shoveled in to fluff out the bundle, and that I wouldn't enjoy it. I ended up loving it, and I'm definitely going to buy the DLC (and likely any more content that may come out for Hacknet in the future).

Hacknet, for lack of better words, is a Unix-based hacking simulator in which you use the combination of a point-and-click interface and a command prompt to explore the mysterious death of a hacker named "Bit." Bit has arranged to send automated messages to you posthumously, giving you leads that are just enough for you to find your way.

Being not much of a programmer, and unfamiliar with Linux and Unix-based command systems (idk man I just look stuff up and punch shit into the Windows 10 command prompt and sometimes it says words back to me), I felt learning to play Hacknet might be too daunting of a task. However, the feeling subsided in less than half an hour, when I was able to navigate through any device's file systems with ease, hopping from device to device, opening ports, cracking passwords, etc. Not long after that was I very immersed in the story (something I have a hard time being in MANY games).

While some aspects of the game can be done through clicking between devices, folders, and apps, other things are seemingly only possible by using the command-line, keeping the game immersive and making you feel, in a sense, accomplished. YOU cracked open all of Macrosoft's ports and got to snoop around in their sensitive files. YOU found a security loophole by exploiting a computer's connected smartphone. YOU made a clean getaway just in time before having your IP traced, clearing the system logs and running for the hills with some juicy new program you can use to hack *even more* devices. And you did it all with your analytical skills and an intuitive command system. In fact, there's even a point in the game where your OS/interface is essentially deleted from your system by another angry hacker, leaving you with a big black command terminal, having to plot through your own computer to restore the deleted files and get yourself back in the game. Just like in real life, each device you access seems like a sum of its parts, even your own.

The IP tracing mechanic is excellent, and pretty much exactly what you'd imagine seeing on some Hollywood hacker's monitor. It keeps the pressure on, even if it is slow at times. RAM management, learning what ports to use when, and being able to type quickly and remember which programs do what are important, and make hacking into each and every system rewarding in its own way, even if it doesn't have quite what you were looking for.

The visual effects are excellent, if a bit cheesy at times. The interface is simple enough that these "glitchy" or "tech-y" effects aren't too jarring unless they need to be, which keeps the game immersive but also fun to watch. I'd advise that anyone with epilepsy be careful with this game at some times - lots of effects are fast or flashy in nature.

The story doesn't seem to thrust itself into your face at all. Save for the occasional automated (but justified) email from Bit, you discover all of the story on your own, and every lead and new piece of information feels genuine and is worth discovering.

Overall, I had a lot of fun with this game. Two complaints (which end up not really being complaints after I explain them):

- The IP map, showing all known devices and their IPs, can get a bit cluttered, and it's easy to forget where one particular computer is on the big web of spinning circles and lines connecting them. The position of an IP address on the map is not always intuitive. However, this could arguably help with immersion, making you feel like you're navigating through a web of IP addresses. It's the internet in its raw form - not catered to your viewing pleasure.

- I'm left wanting more. Not that I didn't get my money's worth, but I want more. But that's something every game should strive for - leaving you wanting more, and not outstaying its welcome.

Challenging, but *very* rewarding command system that makes you feel clever. Decent story that keeps you invested throughout the game. Findable humorous IRC logs, detailing early Internet culture, which I think are ripped straight from Bash.org, meaning they are real logs written by real people. Stereotypical electronic "hacker" soundtrack which helps the atmosphere of the game.

If any of this interests you, definitely get Hacknet, especially if it's in a bundle or on sale.

Hacknet is, by far, the most enthralling and immersive hacking experience I've played to date. Adding the Labirynths expansion, the game excels at managing your stress levels: there are times of low intensity, times of high intensity, and times of crisis-level intensity. There are also times of "dead"-intensity; that is to say, lest you remember some of the basic mechanics of the game, it's possible at a few points to feel like whatever situation you're experiencing is not salvagable. With the emotional rollercoast also comes incredible use of comedic relief, a little extra sanding to take the edge off. 

Some of the best and brightest moments of Hacknet (and it's expansion) are when you'll find yourself laughing at an IRC log or stray text file's contents; some of them are when you'll find yourself scrambling to disconnect from a server before a trace locks in on your system; some of them are just... breathtaking, almost moving moments that could maybe bring you to tears, and yet further more are moments where your morality comes into play. 

I've only played through the game (and it's expansion) once; I understand that, while limited, there are various other paths and routes that the player may choose to take instead. I'm definitely going to play through the game several more times to find some more secrets and goodies. I'm also interested in the upcoming Hacknet Extensions update, which will bring modding tools and workshop functionality to the table, adding even more content. I'm excited as I'll get out.

I will say, however, if you're not particularly technically inclined, it might be a bit difficult to get going, actually. Don't panic though: most of the game's mechanics have reference material readily available in game, so if you ever forget syntax or a naming convention, it's easy to find the solution.

If you're interested in science-fiction action/mystery thrillers, then this is a game for you.

Hacknet is an enjoyable hacking/terminal simulator. That's where the real challenge comes in. I had to stop playing for some months because of a game breaking bug but revisited after a fix and recently completed it. It's better to do this all in one go so your commands and tools are fresh in your mind as you go deeper down the rabbit hole. The story will keep the player interested while the visuals and music do an excellent job of keeping the entire thing exciting. Hacknet is a tight package worth its ten dollar price.

[h1]       *** Disclaimer *** [/h1] [h1] [/h1]
This game does not teach you how to code or hack, it teaches you how to use command line and does not hold your hand. 
[h1] ***  End of Disclaimer ***  [/h1]

Played With: Mouse & Keyboard; Windows 10

[h1]Pros: [/h1]
-No Hand Holding, Learn: The game gives you basic ideas of how to play and what you can do but it on you to learn the commands and how they work if you want to progress and allows you to investigate and mess with whatever you want, you may mess up.
-Investigation (Puzzles): The game presents you with challenges or puzzles and puts you in this I gotta figure out mentality, kind of like one more turn but one more puzzle. 

[h1]Cons: [/h1] 
-You May Mess Up: There aren’t many ways to do that but if you try or you don’t learn enough about the command line you can mess yourself up, for instance I deleted all my system files just to see what happens the first time around, at that point I had no idea how to reverse that; I had to restart. 
-Not For Everyone: This game does not hold your hand and if you aren’t willing to sit down and think about it you may get frustrated. 

[h1]General Thoughts: [/h1]
-This game was something I never knew I wanted but I very much appreciate that I got to play it. It may not be THE hacking game but it’s a great intro to it and I have looked further into it once I was done playing. You won’t find many games like this on steam and if you get a chance grab it.
